To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Borna disease virus infection of rodents causes a variety of behavioral abnormalities and neurochemical changes that are consistent with those observed in human neuropsychiatric disorders, and these abnormalities can occur in the absence of overt clinical signs or histopathological evidence of CNS injury.

(1) Borna disease virus infection of rodents results in a spectrum of behavioral, neuropharmalogical, and neurochemical changes, (2) Borna disease viral infection in rodents is associated with neuroinflammation, (3) Borna disease is associated with neuronal injury, (4) Borna disease in rodents is associated, in some cases, with neuronal cell death, and (5) Borna disease can be used as a model of CNS viral injury.
Borna disease virus (BDV) is an enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-sense RNA virus with an unusual host range that includes birds and mammals.
